SPEAK OUT ACT — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Acme, Inc.

ABOUT THIS DOCUMENT: THE FEDERAL SPEAK OUT ACT, AND HOW IT DIFFERS FROM CALIFORNIA NON-DISPARAGEMENT LAW
This information sheet describes a single federal statute: the Speak Out Act, Pub. L. 117-224 (Dec. 7, 2022), codified at 42 U.S.C. §§ 19401-19404. It is a separate body of law from this corpus's Non-Disparagement Agreement — Information Sheet, which covers California's settlement-agreement disclosure ban (Code Civ. Proc. § 1001), California's broader Silenced No More Act (Gov. Code § 12964.5), and federal labor-law limits on severance non-disparagement clauses under the National Labor Relations Act (29 U.S.C. §§ 157-158). This document does not restate any of that material. Instead, it addresses a narrower question the other document does not reach: whether a nondisclosure or nondisparagement clause signed before a sexual assault or sexual harassment dispute ever arose — for example, in a standard employment agreement, offer letter, or business contract signed when a relationship began, with no dispute yet in sight — can later be enforced in court to silence someone about that dispute once it does arise. Acme, Inc. and Jordan Lee are identified here for reference throughout this document; the document describes federal statutory text and does not itself determine whether the Speak Out Act applies to any specific clause, contract, or dispute between them.

STATUTORY DEFINITIONS: “SEXUAL ASSAULT DISPUTE” AND “SEXUAL HARASSMENT DISPUTE”
The Speak Out Act defines two categories of dispute that trigger its rule. A “sexual assault dispute” means a dispute involving a nonconsensual sexual act or sexual contact, using terms defined in the federal criminal code at 18 U.S.C. § 2246, or a similar applicable Tribal or State law definition, and it expressly includes a dispute where the victim lacked the capacity to consent. A “sexual harassment dispute” means a dispute relating to conduct alleged to constitute sexual harassment under applicable Federal, Tribal, or State law — the statute does not define “sexual harassment” itself; it borrows whatever definition already exists under the law governing the dispute at hand.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "The term “ sexual assault dispute ” means a dispute involving a nonconsensual sexual act or sexual contact, as such terms are defined in section 2246 of title 18 or similar applicable Tribal or State law, including when the victim lacks capacity to consent."
  — 42 U.S.C. § 19402(3) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, Speak Out Act, definition of “sexual assault dispute” (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/42/19402)
  "The term “ sexual harassment dispute ” means a dispute relating to conduct that is alleged to constitute sexual harassment under applicable Federal, Tribal, or State law."
  — 42 U.S.C. § 19402(4) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, Speak Out Act, definition of “sexual harassment dispute” (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/42/19402)
  Known gap: The “sexual assault dispute” definition cross-references 18 U.S.C. § 2246's definitions of “sexual act” and “sexual contact”; that cross-referenced section was not independently fetched or verified in this research — only 42 U.S.C. § 19402's own text, which names it, was fetched and confirmed. The “sexual harassment dispute” definition supplies no federal definition of “sexual harassment” of its own; it points outward to whatever Federal, Tribal, or State law already defines that term for the dispute at hand, so what counts as a covered dispute can vary by jurisdiction and cause of action. Correction to an initial research assumption: the Speak Out Act's Public Law number is Pub. L. 117-224 (Dec. 7, 2022, 136 Stat. 2290), confirmed directly in the statute's own short-title note as fetched from law.cornell.edu — not Pub. L. 117-90, an earlier assumption this document corrects. This is federal law, generally applicable regardless of which state the parties are in, but whether it applies to a specific clause or dispute still turns on facts this document doesn't resolve. This document is informational only and does not itself resolve whether a specific clause is enforceable in a specific case.

STATUTORY DEFINITIONS: “NONDISCLOSURE CLAUSE” AND “NONDISPARAGEMENT CLAUSE”
The statute separately defines the two kinds of clauses it reaches. A “nondisclosure clause” means a provision in a contract or agreement that requires the parties not to disclose or discuss conduct, the existence of a settlement involving conduct, or information covered by the contract or agreement's terms and conditions. A “nondisparagement clause” means a provision in a contract or agreement that requires one or more parties not to make a negative statement about another party relating to the contract, agreement, claim, or case. Both definitions are broad enough to reach many contract types — not only settlement agreements, but also employment agreements, offer letters, severance agreements, and ordinary business or consumer contracts.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "The term “ nondisclosure clause ” means a provision in a contract or agreement that requires the parties to the contract or agreement not to disclose or discuss conduct, the existence of a settlement involving conduct, or information covered by the terms and conditions of the contract or agreement."
  — 42 U.S.C. § 19402(1) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, Speak Out Act, definition of “nondisclosure clause” (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/42/19402)
  "The term “ nondisparagement clause ” means a provision in a contract or agreement that requires 1 or more parties to the contract or agreement not to make a negative statement about another party that relates to the contract, agreement, claim, or case."
  — 42 U.S.C. § 19402(2) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, Speak Out Act, definition of “nondisparagement clause” (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/42/19402)
  Known gap: These definitions are specific to this federal chapter (42 U.S.C. §§ 19401-19404); this document's use of “nondisclosure clause” and “nondisparagement clause” tracks this statute's own wording, which does not necessarily match how similar terms are used in this corpus's separate Non-Disparagement Agreement — Information Sheet or the California statutes it covers. This is federal law, generally applicable regardless of which state the parties are in, but whether a specific contract provision meets these definitions still turns on that provision's own wording. This document is informational only and does not itself resolve whether a specific clause is enforceable in a specific case.

WHAT IS VOIDED: A PREDISPUTE CLAUSE, NOT ANY NONDISCLOSURE OR NONDISPARAGEMENT CLAUSE
The statute's operative rule is narrow and specific about timing. With respect to a sexual assault dispute or sexual harassment dispute, no nondisclosure clause or nondisparagement clause agreed to before the dispute arises is judicially enforceable, in instances where the conduct at issue is alleged to have violated Federal, Tribal, or State law. In plain terms: a confidentiality or non-disparagement clause signed before any dispute existed — such as one included in an employment agreement, offer letter, or standard business contract signed when the relationship began — cannot be enforced in court to block someone from later speaking about a sexual assault or sexual harassment dispute that subsequently arises.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "With respect to a sexual assault dispute or sexual harassment dispute , no nondisclosure clause or nondisparagement clause agreed to before the dispute arises shall be judicially enforceable in instances in which conduct is alleged to have violated Federal, Tribal, or State law."
  — 42 U.S.C. § 19403(a) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, Speak Out Act, limitation on judicial enforceability of a predispute nondisclosure or nondisparagement clause (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/42/19403)
  Known gap: The statute bars “judicial enforceability” specifically — its text does not say the clause is void, illegal, or unenforceable for every purpose; it says a court will not enforce it in this context, which is what a court considers if someone tries to invoke the clause against a person speaking out. The statute does not itself define when a dispute “arises” for timing purposes; that threshold question is not resolved in the statutory text, and no case law addressing it was checked in this research (CourtListener's case-law search was rate-limited/exhausted before this document could be checked there). The rule's effect also requires that the underlying conduct be “alleged to have violated Federal, Tribal, or State law” — a factual and legal threshold this document doesn't resolve for any specific situation. This is federal law, generally applicable regardless of which state the parties are in, but whether it makes a specific clause unenforceable in a specific case still turns on facts this document doesn't resolve. This document is informational only and does not itself resolve whether a specific clause is enforceable in a specific case.

POST-DISPUTE SETTLEMENT AGREEMENTS FALL OUTSIDE THIS FEDERAL BAR
The predispute limitation described above cuts both ways: by its own terms, the statute reaches only a nondisclosure or nondisparagement clause “agreed to before the dispute arises.” A nondisclosure or nondisparagement clause that is instead negotiated and signed after a sexual assault or sexual harassment dispute has already arisen — the typical case of a settlement agreement resolving that specific dispute — is not made judicially unenforceable by this federal statute. The Speak Out Act does not prohibit, restrict, or otherwise address confidentiality or non-disparagement terms in a post-dispute settlement agreement; its text is silent on that category of agreement.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "no nondisclosure clause or nondisparagement clause agreed to before the dispute arises shall be judicially enforceable"
  — 42 U.S.C. § 19403(a) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, Speak Out Act, predispute-timing limit that leaves post-dispute agreements outside the bar (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/42/19403)
  Known gap: This clause's citation is the same statutory subsection as the previous clause (42 U.S.C. § 19403(a)) — it is not independent corroboration, only the flip side of the same predispute/post-dispute line drawn by that subsection's own wording. Separate state-law rules — including, in California, the settlement-agreement disclosure ban and Silenced No More Act covered in this corpus's separate Non-Disparagement Agreement — Information Sheet — may still restrict what a post-dispute settlement agreement can require, even where this federal statute does not; this document does not restate that material, and a reader evaluating a post-dispute settlement agreement should look to that separate document rather than this one. Whether a specific agreement was reached before or after a dispute “arose” is a factual question this document doesn't resolve, and no case law addressing that timing question was checked in this research. This document is informational only and does not itself resolve whether a specific settlement agreement is enforceable in a specific case.

CARVE-OUTS: STATE LAW, PSEUDONYM RULES, AND TRADE SECRETS
The statute preserves three things outside its core rule. First, it doesn't stop a state or locality from enforcing its own, separate law governing nondisclosure or nondisparagement clauses, as long as that state or local law is at least as protective of a person's right to speak freely as this federal statute is. Second, it doesn't override any Federal, State, or Tribal law governing the use of pseudonyms when filing a claim involving a sexual assault or sexual harassment dispute. Third, it doesn't stop an employer and employee from protecting trade secrets or proprietary information.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "Nothing in this chapter shall prohibit a State or locality from enforcing a provision of State law governing nondisclosure or nondisparagement clauses that is at least as protective of the right of an individual to speak freely, as provided by this chapter."
  — 42 U.S.C. § 19403(b) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, Speak Out Act, continued applicability of more-protective state or local law (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/42/19403)
  "the use of pseudonyms in the filing of claims involving sexual assault or sexual harassment disputes."
  — 42 U.S.C. § 19403(c) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, Speak Out Act, continued applicability of pseudonym-filing law (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/42/19403)
  "Nothing in this chapter shall prohibit an employer and an employee from protecting trade secrets or proprietary information."
  — 42 U.S.C. § 19403(d) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, Speak Out Act, trade secret and proprietary information carve-out (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/42/19403)
  Known gap: All three citations below are subsections of the same statutory section as the two clauses above (42 U.S.C. § 19403(b), (c), and (d)) — they are treated as one source with those clauses, not independent corroboration of each other. The “at least as protective” standard in subsection (b) is not itself defined by any measurable criterion in the statutory text; how a specific state or local law compares is not resolved here. The trade-secret carve-out in subsection (d) does not define “trade secrets or proprietary information” — neither term is defined anywhere in this chapter. This is federal law, generally applicable regardless of which state the parties are in, but whether a specific state law is “at least as protective,” or a specific clause protects a genuine trade secret, are questions this document doesn't resolve. This document is informational only and does not itself resolve whether a specific clause is enforceable in a specific case.

APPLICABILITY: CLAIMS FILED ON OR AFTER DECEMBER 7, 2022
The statute applies to a claim filed under Federal, State, or Tribal law on or after December 7, 2022 — the date the Speak Out Act was signed into law. The trigger for applicability is the filing date of the claim, not the date the underlying nondisclosure or nondisparagement clause was originally signed. That means a clause signed years before December 7, 2022 — for example, in an older employment agreement — can still be reached by this statute's predispute rule if the sexual assault or sexual harassment claim to which it relates is filed on or after that date.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "This chapter shall apply with respect to a claim that is filed under Federal, State, or Tribal law on or after December 7, 2022"
  — 42 U.S.C. § 19404 (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, Speak Out Act, applicability to claims filed on or after December 7, 2022 (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/42/19404)
  Known gap: The statute doesn't define what counts as a claim being “filed” for this purpose — whether that means a civil lawsuit, an administrative charge, an internal complaint, or something else is not resolved by the statutory text, and no case law addressing that question was checked in this research (CourtListener's case-law search returned a 429 rate-limit response, 125/day exhausted, before this document could be checked there; given how recent this 2022 statute is, case law interpreting it may also simply be scarce). This applicability provision uses a different timing concept (“filed”) from the predispute-clause rule's own timing concept (“before the dispute arises”); the two dates need not coincide, and this document doesn't resolve how they interact in every case. This is federal law, generally applicable regardless of which state the parties are in, but whether a specific claim was “filed” on or after December 7, 2022 is a factual question this document doesn't resolve. This document is informational only and does not itself resolve whether a specific clause is enforceable in a specific case.

CLOSING NOTE AND RELATIONSHIP TO THIS CORPUS'S OTHER NON-DISPARAGEMENT DOCUMENT
This information sheet describes the federal Speak Out Act (42 U.S.C. §§ 19401-19404) as it applies to a predispute nondisclosure or nondisparagement clause relating to a sexual assault or sexual harassment dispute. It does not describe, restate, or duplicate this corpus's separate Non-Disparagement Agreement — Information Sheet, which covers different legal topics: California's settlement-agreement disclosure ban, California's Silenced No More Act, federal NLRA limits on severance non-disparagement clauses, general contract-law enforceability, and the confidentiality-versus-non-disparagement distinction. A reader evaluating a specific clause, contract, or dispute should consult both documents as relevant, along with the statutory text itself and, where appropriate, a licensed attorney, since neither document determines the outcome for Jordan Lee's or Acme, Inc.'s specific situation.

Prepared regarding: Acme, Inc. and Jordan Lee
Date: September 1, 2026
